The ethics committee considered his defense "full of internal contractions" and found him in breach of the Lords Code of Conduct. Two other lawmakers, Lord Moonie and Lord Snape, were found not to have breached the code. Only the Queen can permanently strip a lord of his title. Both Taylor and Truscott are associated with the governing Labor Party. Thomas Taylor joined the House of Lords, the upper house of parliament, in 1978. Peter Truscott got his baronage in 2004. Their historic suspension comes a day after the speaker of the House of Commons, the lower house of parliament, was forced to resign -- the first such resignation in more than 300 years. ## UK Lords suspended in “cash-for-influence” scandal, first such punishment since 1642

**London —** Two members of Britain’s House of Lords were suspended in 2009 after a “cash-for-influence” scandal raised fresh questions about lobbying, parliamentary ethics and the unelected upper chamber.

The case began when **The Sunday Times** published an undercover investigation in which reporters posed as lobbyists seeking help to amend legislation. Four Labour peers were drawn into the investigation: **Lord Peter Truscott**, **Lord Thomas Taylor of Blackburn**, **Lord Lewis Moonie** and **Lord Peter Snape**.

The newspaper alleged that some peers appeared willing to use their parliamentary positions to help secure changes to laws in return for fees. The allegations prompted an inquiry by the House of Lords’ **Privileges Committee**, which concluded that two of the peers — Truscott and Taylor — had breached the chamber’s rules.

In May 2009, the Lords voted to suspend **Lord Truscott** and **Lord Taylor of Blackburn** for several months. It was widely reported as the **first suspension of members of the House of Lords since 1642**, making the punishment historically significant as well as politically damaging.

### The undercover sting

According to the Sunday Times investigation, reporters secretly recorded meetings with peers after claiming to represent a business client that wanted amendments made to proposed legislation.

Lord Truscott, a former Labour energy minister, was reported to have discussed helping with amendments and using contacts in government. Lord Taylor, a veteran Labour peer and former local council leader, was also accused of suggesting he could assist in influencing legislation for payment.

The Lords’ inquiry found that both men had been willing to enter arrangements that would breach the chamber’s rules, which prohibit peers from accepting payment in return for parliamentary services.

The committee said their conduct had failed to meet the standard expected of members of the House. In the language of the Lords’ code, peers were expected to act on their “personal honour.”

### Who were the lords involved?

**Lord Peter Truscott**  
Truscott was a Labour peer who had served as a government minister in the Department of Trade and Industry and later in the Department for Energy. His background in energy policy was relevant because the undercover reporters were seeking help on legislative issues affecting business interests.

**Lord Taylor of Blackburn**  
Taylor was a long-serving Labour figure from Lancashire and a former leader of Blackburn council. In the Lords, he was known for his political experience and business contacts. The investigation alleged he discussed using his position to help clients for substantial fees.

**Lord Lewis Moonie**  
Moonie was a former Labour MP and defence minister. He was also investigated after meeting the undercover reporters, but the Lords’ committee did not recommend suspension. He was criticized, but the sanctions imposed on Truscott and Taylor were the most severe.

**Lord Peter Snape**  
Snape, another Labour peer and former MP, was also caught up in the inquiry. Like Moonie, he faced scrutiny over his discussions with the reporters but was not suspended.

### “Cash for amendments”

The scandal became known as a “cash-for-influence” or “cash-for-amendments” affair because it centered on whether peers were prepared to take money to help change legislation.

At the time, the allegations were especially damaging because the House of Lords operated largely on trust and self-regulation. Unlike elected MPs, peers did not face voters, and the case intensified calls for tougher rules on lobbying and outside financial interests.

The scandal also came during a broader period of public anger over political standards in Britain. Just months later, the UK Parliament would be engulfed by the MPs’ expenses scandal, further eroding confidence in Westminster.

### Historic punishment

The suspension of Truscott and Taylor was notable not only for the misconduct findings but also because of its rarity. The last comparable suspension from the Lords was said to have occurred in **1642**, during the turbulent years leading into the English Civil War.

For a chamber often criticized as antiquated and resistant to reform, the 2009 vote was a dramatic assertion that peers could be punished for abusing — or appearing willing to abuse — their parliamentary role.

Both suspended peers denied wrongdoing, but the Lords concluded that their conduct was serious enough to warrant removal from the chamber for the remainder of the parliamentary session.

The scandal left a lasting mark on debates over lobbying transparency, the role of money in politics and the future of Britain’s unelected upper house.

# The House of Lords “cash for amendments” case: the Sunday Times sting, the ethics inquiry, and why police brought no charges

In 2009 the House of Lords was shaken by one of the most serious parliamentary standards controversies in its modern history: allegations that peers were prepared to use their positions to influence legislation in return for payment. The affair, widely described as a “cash for amendments” scandal, centred on four Labour peers — Lord Taylor of Blackburn, Lord Truscott, Lord Moonie and Lord Snape — and began with an undercover investigation by *The Sunday Times*.

The case led to an inquiry by the Lords’ standards authorities, unprecedented disciplinary action against two peers, and a police investigation that ultimately ended without criminal charges.

## The Sunday Times sting

The controversy began in January 2009 when *The Sunday Times* published the results of an undercover operation. Reporters posed as lobbyists acting for a fictitious business client seeking changes to legislation. They approached several members of the House of Lords, testing whether peers would be willing to help secure amendments or otherwise influence parliamentary business in exchange for consultancy fees.

The newspaper alleged that some peers appeared willing to use their parliamentary access and influence for payment. The sums discussed reportedly ran into thousands of pounds a month, with the total value of potential retainers reaching substantial annual amounts.

The key figures named were:

- **Lord Taylor of Blackburn**, a Labour peer and former teacher who had long experience in the Lords.
- **Lord Truscott**, a Labour peer and former minister.
- **Lord Moonie**, a Labour peer and former defence minister.
- **Lord Snape**, a Labour peer and former MP.

The peers denied wrongdoing to varying degrees, and the central question became whether their conversations with undercover reporters amounted merely to imprudent talk or to a willingness to breach parliamentary rules by taking money to influence legislation.

## Rules on paid advocacy

At the heart of the case was the Lords’ prohibition on “paid advocacy.” Members of the House of Lords are permitted to have outside interests and paid consultancies, provided they declare them properly. However, they are not allowed to accept payment in return for parliamentary services, such as tabling amendments, asking questions, speaking in debates, or otherwise seeking to influence proceedings on behalf of a paying client.

The scandal therefore raised a fundamental issue: whether peers had crossed the line from offering general political advice into selling parliamentary influence.

## The Lords ethics committee investigation

Following the newspaper revelations, the House of Lords launched an internal inquiry through its standards and privileges machinery. The investigation examined transcripts, recordings, and the conduct of the four peers.

The Lords’ Committee for Privileges — acting on the findings of its sub-committee — reached different conclusions about the different peers.

### Lord Taylor of Blackburn

The committee found that **Lord Taylor had breached the House of Lords Code of Conduct**. It concluded that he had expressed willingness to assist the undercover reporters’ supposed client in ways that would have involved parliamentary activity in return for payment.

The findings were particularly damaging because they suggested not simply a failure to declare an interest, but a readiness to engage in paid advocacy — one of the clearest prohibitions in parliamentary ethics.

### Lord Truscott

The committee also found that **Lord Truscott had breached the Code of Conduct**. It concluded that his discussions with the undercover reporters indicated a willingness to help influence legislation for reward.

Like Lord Taylor, he was found to have failed to meet the standard of conduct expected of members of the House.

### Lord Moonie

The committee took a different view of **Lord Moonie**. Although his conversations with the undercover reporters were criticised, the committee did not find that he had agreed to carry out paid advocacy or that he had breached the code in the same way as Taylor and Truscott.

He was therefore not subjected to the same disciplinary sanction.

### Lord Snape

Similarly, **Lord Snape** was not found to have committed the kind of breach established against Taylor and Truscott. His comments were scrutinised and criticised in the wider political fallout, but the committee did not conclude that he had agreed to sell parliamentary services.

## Unprecedented suspensions

The Lords’ response was historically significant. In May 2009, the House voted to suspend **Lord Taylor of Blackburn** and **Lord Truscott** from the House for several months.

The suspensions were widely reported as the first such disciplinary exclusions of peers for centuries. They marked a turning point in how the Lords handled misconduct, demonstrating that the House was willing to impose serious sanctions for breaches of its standards rules.

The case also intensified pressure for broader reform of parliamentary ethics, coming at a time when public confidence in Westminster was already under severe strain because of the MPs’ expenses scandal.

## Police investigation and decision not to prosecute

Alongside the Lords inquiry, the matter was referred to the police. Investigators considered whether the peers’ conduct might amount to a criminal offence, including possible corruption-related offences.

However, the police ultimately decided not to bring charges. The decision reflected the high threshold required for criminal prosecution. While the Lords committee could judge whether members had breached parliamentary standards, a criminal case would have required evidence capable of proving beyond reasonable doubt that a specific offence had been committed.

The absence of charges did not mean that the conduct was endorsed or that the internal findings were overturned. Rather, it highlighted the distinction between:

- **parliamentary discipline**, which concerns breaches of the House’s own rules and standards; and
- **criminal prosecution**, which requires proof of a defined criminal offence to the required legal standard.

In the end, the police and prosecuting authorities concluded that the available evidence did not justify criminal proceedings.

## Significance of the case

The “cash for amendments” affair became one of the most prominent Lords standards cases of the period. Its significance lay in several areas.

First, it exposed public concern about lobbying and access to lawmakers. The idea that unelected legislators might be willing to help paying clients alter legislation struck at the credibility of the parliamentary process.

Second, the case demonstrated the limitations and importance of self-regulation. The Lords was able to investigate and punish breaches of its own code, but the controversy also raised questions about whether internal disciplinary systems were enough.

Third, it showed the legal gap between unethical parliamentary behaviour and criminal corruption. Conduct can be judged improper, dishonourable or in breach of parliamentary rules without necessarily meeting the test for prosecution.

Finally, the suspensions of Lord Taylor and Lord Truscott helped set a precedent for tougher enforcement of standards in the House of Lords.

## Conclusion

The case involving Lord Taylor, Lord Truscott, Lord Moonie and Lord Snape remains a landmark in the history of parliamentary ethics. Triggered by a *Sunday Times* sting, it led to severe criticism of the way some peers discussed paid lobbying work, formal findings of misconduct against Taylor and Truscott, and unprecedented suspensions from the House of Lords.

Yet the police decision not to bring criminal charges underlined the difference between political or ethical culpability and criminal liability. The affair damaged public trust, sharpened scrutiny of lobbying, and became part of the wider debate about transparency, accountability and reform in Britain’s unelected second chamber.
